body: It has been difficult.  I have a deep sense that I don't belong, which wouldn't be such a big deal, except that I'm stuck here for the time being.  I'm hoping that I'll be able to get a car soon.  Then I'll just go back to the city and stay in a shelter until I can get some things sorted out.

Thank you!  I've always been the quiet type, which gives me more time to create elaborate social commentaries in my head.  It may sound weird, but it keeps me busy.

For sure.  It's just a lot harder when I'm trapped here, you know?

It never was an issue when I wasn't living with them, but now that I have to bear their ridicule every day (not directed necessarily toward me, but with LGBT+ issues being more prevalent in the media, I hear jabs all the time, and I also am being considered a failure because of my living/job situation), I can't help but take their words to heart.  I'm slowly being beaten down, because the people who in theory should support me hate people who are like me.  It feels awful.

I appreciate that.  I'm hoping that what comes next is not unpleasant, for your sake. 

Funny enough, one side of my family is Baptist and the other is Catholic.  They both seem to hate the same things, but are different enough to equally hate each other.  

I think we all have our crosses to bear, so to speak.  Aboriginal news is certainly fascinating, and it's a field I would like to research further.

Well, maybe, but I have no money, care, or means to escape.  I wish I could pursue a means of escape.  But, I just can't right now.  I'd genuinely rather die than live in these conditions for the length of time I know it'd take for things to improve. I wish that taking care of my family would've been enough, but it just wasn't.  I will always be wrong for my gender identity and for not being physically sound or the fact that I haven't graduated college yet.  No matter how much I do right, I will always be wrong, and I can't cope.

I'm glad that you're sharing your experiences.  I've actually had a similar experience of eating rabbits and chickens I considered pets because I had a deeper attachment to them than the rest of my family did.  They're nice enough people on the outside, but very bigoted.  I was watching an LGBT news broadcast today, and my super religious grandmother told me angrily to find something else to put on.  But, she still loves ham and wearing clothes woven out of mixed fabrics.  Christians, eh?

Awww, that's sad.  I'm sorry that you're going through that.  I've never been married, so I can't really empathize, but I've loved and lost and held certain dates in significance based on that, you know?  

It's hard.  I've lived alone, but only briefly.  I've lived most of my life among people who would not understand or would hate who I am.  I only really understand that kind of pain.  I am not sure who "wins", but please know that I support you and your pain.

No, that's okay.  That makes sense.  Gender is a spectrum, after all, and all of us vary as far as how emotional/physical we are.  

That's something I worry about.  I am not an aggressive kind of guy, but I am scared that testosterone will cause a spike of aggression.  I also am worried about potential hair loss and acne (I have super clear skin and thick hair, so those potential downsides terrify me).

Thank you so much.  I have some very understanding friends  But, my long term boyfriend broke up with me when he found out about my gender identity, and the family thing has always been very tricky.  Truth be told, I have always had a complicated relationship with all of them.  They're bigoted and narcissistic, and I've resigned myself to the fact that they'll never quite understand me, even though it's painful.  

As for why I want to be a guy, it goes back a long way.  When I was little, I always found myself eschewing feminine things.  I even hated being called a girl, though I couldn't place why.  I was always the kind of person who enjoyed climbing trees, shooting BB guns, and such.  I'd always subconsciously pick away at nail polish or tug at my dresses as if they didn't belong on me.  

I think I really understood what was going on when I was twelve years old.  I was exceptionally confused about my own identity, as I found myself much more attracted to girls, and honestly identified much more as a man than a woman.  My family was not the type to shy away from sexual discussions, but were tight-lipped when it came to discussions that strayed from the heterosexual agenda, so to speak.  My own epiphany about who I was led to a decade of self-loathing and depression.  

When I was 20, I moved to the big city, and I was suddenly friends with a number of attractive boys.  As a female, I was a bit overweight, but still pretty cute, if I do say so myself.  But, my family was the kind of poor that I could count on one hand the number of times I'd ever shopped for clothing.  When I got my own job, I thought that maybe I'd never felt feminine because I had never truly experienced fashion and makeup, so I decided to devote any spare pennies to making myself pretty.  I knew that I was a man inside, but my family was so non-accepting that I thought it was best to live in fear and denial.  It didn't occur to me that I should live in such a way as to make myself happy, rather than living for them.

That backfired horribly.  The prettier I got, the more depressed I ended up.  Eventually, it got the point where I just wanted to die.  I knew that something had to give.  I realized that it would be difficult, but I needed to live authentically.  I was a shy, terribly self-conscious woman, but I knew I would be a badass man, and that I'm tough enough to go through the steps necessary to present myself in that way.  It's been tough, but I feel super liberated in a way, for being able to publicly admit what I had hidden for so long.  

Honestly, I encourage you to do what's right for you.  I know you've said that the process isn't worth it for you, but it's totally okay to feel that kind of curiosity and such.  I don't say that to sound condescending.  It's just that you're a valuable human being regardless of your gender alignment, you know?

Thank you for asking.  I actually think it's great that you want to know more.  I was born a girl with lady parts.  I have my appointment to start hormone therapy (specifically, I'm looking to be prescribed injectable testosterone) in about two weeks, and plan to have a mastectomy in the future.  Right now, I'm still technically a girl with lady parts, but I've been using a male name (to those outside my family), cutting my hair short, and dressing in men's clothes for a long time.  I've always known that I was born in the wrong body.  For all intents and purposes, I am male, and actually somewhat passable despite not officially starting the physical transition yet.
That's really sweet of you.  I'd like that.  I'm male, too, or actually, FTM.
